extracted.intended_audience: British public, Parliament, electors, and young English readers (readers of a political/personal pamphlet)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on how to speak, write, and act in public life: emphasises truthfulness, restraint of speech, silent work over performative oratory, and seeking facts rather than rhetorical applause. Aimed at citizens, politicians, and young people forming character and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a correct image of the fact / truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Get, by ... the silent intimation of your own eyesight and understanding given you direct out of Heaven ... a correct image of the fact in question, as God and Nature have made it: that is the one thing needful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute popular consensus, parliamentary votes, or eloquent pleading for an actual comprehension of facts; voting, perorating and reporting will not alter the thing itself. If your thought images the fact falsely, your actions will fail because 'the fact will silently resist you.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the impalpable liar — rhetorical commonplaces and cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the 'impalpable liar, whose tongue articulates mere accepted commonplaces, cants and babblement' — the man who speaks conventional phrases to be admired rather than to convey truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such speech indicates an inner mind that has 'run all to seed' and becomes a 'giver of falsities'; admiration from crowds only deepens intellectual and moral decay and leads toward ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject stump-oratory and speaking for applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not become a 'Stump-Orator' or 'Public Orator' appealing to the vulgar with platforms, parliaments, and applause; public eloquence that seeks applause is spiritually deadening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public speaking aimed at popularity produces 'words without wisdom' and a 'galvanic life' of performative loquacity; it sacrifices inner veracity and honest thought in exchange for seats and rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer silence; preserve and fructify ideas before speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can keep an idea unspoken it remains richer: 'The idea you have once spoken, if it even were an idea, is no longer yours... Better keep your idea while you can.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence lets ideas circulate inwardly and mature into more effective action or more concise expression later. Speaking prematurely drains an idea's life and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise work and action over literary fame or speech
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak or to write is not necessarily your duty; 'to work she did' — Nature orders work rather than literary display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talent for literature should not supplant practical, silent activity. The author counsels young people to 'work, work; whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it,—with the hand of a man, not of a phantasm.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid performing for appearance — oppose 'eye-service'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not act merely 'with a view to their being seen' — eye-service reduces genuine fruitfulness and nobleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing for spectators makes actions superficial and corrupts motive; genuine achievement is produced by unseen, sincere effort rather than display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eschew wit that substitutes for wisdom and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Witty,—above all, oh be not witty: none of us is bound to be witty, under penalties; to be wise and true we all are, under the terriblest penalties!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit for its own sake is shallow and can distract from commitment to truth; prefer frankness and wisdom even at social or rhetorical cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of relying on reported speeches / mass-mediated thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary parliaments with reporters produce a distorted copy of actual thought: 'And upon that latter you are to act;—with what success, do you expect?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that what is recorded and broadcast is often a 'double-distilled falsity' far removed from the speaker's wisest thought; policy and action based on such distortions are likely to fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise Nature's moral accounting — consequences of truth and falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature 'keeps silently a most exact Savings-bank, and official register' — Creditor for acts of veracity and Debtor for falsities; all will be exacted in due time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsehoods and errors accumulate moral and practical liabilities which will bring ruin or spiritual loss; monetary gain can itself be a form of doom if it fosters vice and loss of soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise factual inquiry over constitutional or rhetorical reform
rubrics_metrics.description: After constitutional improvements, the primary task remains 'to ascertain what the truth of your question, in Nature, really is!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional reform and parliamentary eloquence are insufficient without an accurate understanding of facts; political procedures must be grounded in reality to succeed.
